title: Bram and the Typewriter
premise: In 1911, Tamsin Eriksen, an indentured pearl diver's son in a coastal trading port, is ordered to type and seal a letter that quietly names his own family among conspirators planning to seize the company's fleet and drown a rival's divers in debt. When the letter's intended recipient is found dead, Tamsin steals it and the company's battered typewriter, the only machine whose impressions match the incriminating pages. Hunted by the company's fixers and distrusted by his own kin, he must gather testimony from divers, clerks, and one dying conspirator, typing the record in secret. In the end he mails copies to newspapers and a magistrate before the company can burn the archive — winning justice, but at the cost of his indenture, his hometown, and any chance of an ordinary life.
about_author: Cyrus Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers and indenture papers along the pearl coasts. Bram and the Typewriter is his second novel of labor, ink, and the people history forgets to record.

chapters.title: The Ledger Room
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Sixteen and indentured, Tamsin keeps his head down copying manifests in the trading company's ledger room, hiding his quick fingers and quicker mind. A clerk's cruelty and a diver's drowning establish the company's casual brutality. Beat: quiet endurance, the ache of being owned on paper.

chapters.title: A Letter in Someone Else's Hand
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Ordered to type and seal an unsigned letter, Tamsin reads names he knows — his father among them — in a plot to rig debts and seize the fleet. Terrified, he seals it anyway. That night the recipient is found drowned. Beat: dread, the first irreversible choice.

chapters.title: What the Keys Remember
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Realizing the typewriter's impressions can convict or exonerate, Tamsin steals it and the original letter, hiding them in the divers' drying sheds. The fixer Vos begins asking questions door to door. Beat: fear sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Salt and Silence
chapters.summary: Father Eriksen's POV. At sea, Tamsin's father weighs the debt that binds him to the conspiracy against the divers already dying of it. He says nothing to his son, believing silence is protection. Beat: love expressed as concealment, guilt settling like silt.

chapters.title: The Clerk Who Talked
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A drunken ex-clerk confirms the scheme and gives Tamsin a torn half-ledger as proof — then vanishes before he can testify. Vos finds the shed searched and narrows his suspicion to the ledger room boys. Beat: hope and loss in the same hour.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Sister Maren's POV. Tamsin's sister discovers his cache and, rather than betray him, helps him type testimony pages by candlelight. Their uneasy alliance rekindles a sibling bond worn thin by years of survival. Beat: belonging found in complicity.

chapters.title: The Dying Confession
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin reaches the conspiracy's architect, now poisoned by his own partners, and takes his dictated confession on the typewriter as Vos closes in. They escape through the oyster beds at low tide. Beat: the record nearly complete, the hunter nearly upon him.

chapters.title: Burn the Archive
chapters.summary: Vos's POV. Vos burns the company's files to erase the trail and corners the Eriksen family, offering Tamsin's father a bargain: the son and the machine, or the whole family's ruin. Beat: cold, procedural menace; the trap snapping shut.

chapters.title: The Night Mail
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. In the climax, Tamsin and Maren race the morning tide to mail confession, half-ledger, and typed copies to a magistrate and three newspapers while Vos hunts them through the warehouse district. Father Eriksen turns on the conspirators to buy his children time and is badly wounded. Beat: desperate, breathless sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Record Remains
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Months later: the company is indicted, the indentures voided, Vos fled. The family leaves the port for a town where no one knows their name; Tamsin keeps the typewriter, its keys worn to his fingers. Justice came, but exile is its price. Beat: bittersweet resolution — a self written, at last, in his own hand.
